readerTitle: Six restaurants, one owner, too many phone calls
caseNote: 가상 사례 (6개 매장 레스토랑 그룹과 중앙 주방, 3개국 예약 소프트웨어 회사) · 단원 개념 적용 레슨
insight: 조직을 짤 때는 사람이 아니라 일을 나눈다. 일마다 규모에서 이득을 보는지, 고객 가까이에서 이득을 보는지 묻고 그에 따라 중앙과 현장에 둔다.
misconception: 조직 구조는 기능형이든 사업부형이든 하나를 골라 회사 전체에 똑같이 적용해야 한다.

sources.text: 조직 설계의 표준 개념 (기능형·사업부형 구조, 집권화·분권화)
모든 사례는 설명용 가상 사례이며 수치는 쓰지 않음

factChecks.note: 모든 사례는 가상이며 통계나 실제 기업 정보를 쓰지 않았습니다. 구매를 한곳에 모으면 물량 할인을 받기 쉽다는 일반론만 썼으니, 과장된 표현이 없는지 검토하세요.
적용 레슨이므로 새 개념을 넣지 않았습니다. PPL-09-01(기능형 vs 사업부형), PPL-09-02(집권화 vs 분권화)의 용어와 정의가 개념 레슨 본문과 일치하는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Six restaurants, one owner, too many phone calls
body: Maya opened one restaurant. Eight years later she runs six. Her phone rings all day: a broken fryer, a cook who quit, a supplier who raised prices at one site but not the others.
Each restaurant buys its own produce. Every hire still needs her approval. Something has to change. The real question is which work goes where.

image.label: A restaurant owner surrounded by six small restaurants, all calling her
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 가운데 휴대폰을 든 지친 식당 주인, 주변에 분위기가 서로 다른 작은 식당 6곳이 있고 각 식당에서 말풍선(프라이어, 사람, 영수증 아이콘)이 그녀에게 날아옴. 실제 브랜드나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: How should Maya organize the group?
body: She wants to keep each restaurant's personality and stop doing everything herself. Which setup do you choose?

options.text: Put each general manager fully in charge of their restaurant, including buying and hiring
options.feedback: This is a **divisional** setup by location. Managers move fast and own their results, but six separate buyers give up the volume discounts one buyer could get.

options.text: Share buying, payroll and recruiting across the group. Leave the floor and daily specials to each manager
options.feedback: A hybrid: **functional** where scale pays, **divisional** where the guests are. You keep the discounts and the local judgment.

options.text: Build head-office teams for kitchen, service and buying that run all six
options.feedback: A pure **functional** setup gives consistency. But a service director three restaurants away can't fix a slow Friday night in time.

cards.title: Sort the work, not the people.
body: Maya's problem isn't that she has six restaurants. It's that every kind of work lands in the same place: her desk.

Some work gets better when one team does it for everyone. Buying cooking oil for six kitchens is cheaper than buying it six times. Other work gets worse the farther it sits from the guest. Nobody at head office can tell when table nine is unhappy.

cards.title: Functional vs divisional, one job at a time
body: A **functional** structure groups people by skill: all buyers together, all finance together. A **divisional** structure groups them by unit, here each restaurant.
Maya doesn't have to pick one for the whole company. For each job she asks one question: does this gain from *scale*, or from being *close to the guest*?

image.label: Two columns sorting restaurant tasks into scale and close to guest
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 열 "Gains from scale"(창고·저울 아이콘), 오른쪽 열 "Gains from being close"(손님 테이블 아이콘). 가운데에서 업무 카드들이 양쪽으로 분류되어 날아감. 차분한 색, 로고 없음.

cards.title: Where Maya put each job
body: Most jobs sorted in a minute. The menu was harder.

breakdown.label: Buying and suppliers
breakdown.detail: One buyer negotiates for six kitchens

breakdown.label: Recruiting pipeline
breakdown.detail: One list of cooks ready to start

breakdown.label: Shift schedules
breakdown.detail: Managers see their own busy nights

breakdown.label: Fixing guest problems
breakdown.detail: Decided at the table, on the spot

cards.title: Who makes the sauces?
body: Maya opens a central kitchen. It makes sauces, stocks and doughs, and a van delivers to all six sites each morning.
Two head chefs want to keep making their own. What rule do you set?

options.text: Any restaurant can opt out whenever it wants
options.feedback: **Decentralizing** gives chefs freedom, but the central kitchen runs on volume. Each opt-out raises the cost per batch for everyone else.

options.text: The central kitchen makes shared basics. Each restaurant makes its signature dishes in-house
options.feedback: This **centralizes** what needs volume and consistency and **decentralizes** what makes each place different. The rule exists before the argument starts.

options.text: Everything must come from the central kitchen
options.feedback: Full **centralization** gives the lowest cost and the most consistency, but chefs lose the dishes guests come for, and some may leave.

cards.title: A hybrid needs written decision rights.
body: Mixed structures break in the gaps. Buying is central, but a manager wants tomatoes from a local farm. Who decides? Write it down: who decides, who must be asked, and who just gets told.
Timing matters too. With two restaurants, a head office is mostly extra cost. Central teams pay off once there's enough volume to share.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: You sell booking software in three countries. Each country team runs its own customer support, help articles and pricing.
Support quality varies a lot, and engineers get the same bug report three times. What do you change?

options.text: Share one bug queue and support toolkit. Keep pricing and local sales in each country
options.feedback: **Functional** where scale pays, **divisional** where markets differ. One queue fixes bugs once, while local teams keep prices and language right.

options.text: Leave it alone. Each country knows its users best
options.feedback: **Decentralization** keeps local speed, but engineers keep paying for three queues, and users in one country wait for a fix another already has.

options.text: Move everything, including pricing, to one headquarters
options.feedback: One price list is simpler, but competitors and budgets differ by country. **Centralizing** pricing trades local fit for neatness.

cards.title: Sort each job by where it works best.
body: **Used in this lesson:** *Functional vs divisional*, to group work by skill when scale pays and by unit when closeness to customers pays. *Centralize or decentralize*, to decide which choices sit at the center and which stay local.
**Try it today:** list ten decisions your business makes every week. Mark each one *scale* or *close to the customer*. Does it sit where your mark says it should?
